title: HippoTune: A Hippocampal Associative Loop–Inspired Fine-Tuning Method for Continual Learning
claim: Prior methods retrieve once per layer; ours loops retrieval repeatedly within each layer to integrate multiple signals.
layout: 2 side-by-side panels, left-to-right flow, green recurrent loop arrow on right
description: Two dashed-border panels sit side by side. The left panel, 'Classic PEFT-CL framework', shows a linear flow. A feature block h^(l-1) feeds into a light-blue ViT^(l) box that holds a prompt block v_t^(l). Below, an input x_rep goes into a gray 'parameter pool' ellipse, and an arrow runs up from the pool to the prompt. The output is h^(l). The right panel, 'HippoTune: Latent Deliberation', has the same layout with two changes. A thick green circular arrow labeled 'Recurrent Retrieval' wraps around the parameter pool. The output is a stack of several h_t^(l) blocks combined by a ⊕ sign into h^(l). Yellow 3D-style blocks and blue boxes carry the notation. The green loop draws the eye first.

abstract: Studies have shown that catastrophic forgetting primarily stems from the difficulty of reactivating old memories; although parameter-efficient fine-tuning can mitigate forgetting while keeping most model parameters frozen, it still falls short in fully reawakening knowledge of prior tasks. In contrast, humans can efficiently retrieve and flexibly integrate existing experiences when learning new tasks, thereby maintaining stable performance on earlier ones. During cognition, the hippocampal EC–DG–CA3–CA1 circuit engages in multiple rounds of associative recall, and its pattern-separation and memory-completion mechanisms excel at activating historical information. Inspired by this mechanism, we propose HippoTune, a latent-space iterative retrieval strategy that embeds a query–retrieve–feedback loop within each Transformer layer. Starting from the hidden state as an initial query, the model performs a few rounds of soft key–value retrieval, projects the retrieved signals back into the query, and updates it iteratively until convergence or a preset iteration limit. Theoretically, we show this process implements a Krylov-style polynomial approximation, equivalent to a differentiable second-order preconditioner, thereby deepening retrieval in a principled way. Empirically, HippoTune outperforms classical buffer-free PEFT-CL methods by 5–8\% in accuracy across three vision benchmarks, while reducing training FLOPs by 50\%, effectively mitigating forgetting under tight compute constraints. Code is available at: https://github.com/yan4xi1/HippoTune.
